questions.category: DBA Foundations, Architecture, and Service Management
questions.question: What are the primary responsibilities of a production DBA?
questions.preferred_answer: A production DBA protects availability, recoverability, performance, security, and integrity. Typical work includes provisioning, configuration, access control, backup and restore, monitoring, capacity planning, patching, change review, incident response, documentation, and coordination with developers, infrastructure, security, and business owners.

questions.category: DBA Foundations, Architecture, and Service Management
questions.question: Differentiate an instance, a database, and a schema.
questions.preferred_answer: An instance is the running database engine and its memory or processes. A database is a managed collection of data and metadata. A schema is a logical namespace or ownership boundary inside a database. Exact boundaries vary by product, so a strong answer names the target platform before applying the terms.
questions.source_title: Microsoft Learn - SQL Server Database Engine
questions.integrity_note: Original MapIT preparation question; not an employer assessment leak.

questions.category: DBA Foundations, Architecture, and Service Management
questions.question: What is the difference between logical and physical database architecture?
questions.preferred_answer: Logical architecture describes tables, schemas, relationships, constraints, views, and transactions. Physical architecture describes files, pages, blocks, logs, memory, processes, and storage placement. DBAs connect the two because logical design choices affect physical I/O, recovery, concurrency, and capacity.
questions.integrity_note: Original MapIT preparation question; not an employer assessment leak.

questions.category: DBA Foundations, Architecture, and Service Management
questions.question: Explain ACID properties from an operational perspective.
questions.preferred_answer: Atomicity prevents partial transactions, consistency preserves declared rules, isolation controls visibility among concurrent transactions, and durability preserves committed work after failure. A DBA supports these through transaction settings, logging, recovery, constraints, storage reliability, and correct application usage.
questions.integrity_note: Original MapIT preparation question; not an employer assessment leak.

questions.category: DBA Foundations, Architecture, and Service Management
questions.question: How do OLTP and analytical workloads differ for a DBA?
questions.preferred_answer: OLTP favors many short, selective, concurrent transactions with predictable latency. Analytical workloads favor scans, joins, aggregation, parallelism, and throughput. Administration differs in indexing, memory, storage layout, concurrency controls, maintenance windows, workload isolation, and capacity planning.
questions.source_title: Microsoft Learn - Index Architecture and Design Guide
questions.integrity_note: Original MapIT preparation question; not an employer assessment leak.

questions.category: DBA Foundations, Architecture, and Service Management
questions.question: Why is normalization still relevant to database administration?
questions.preferred_answer: Normalization reduces update anomalies and duplicated facts, improving integrity and maintainability. It can increase joins and operational complexity, so DBAs evaluate normalization together with workload, indexing, partitioning, caching, and reporting needs rather than treating the highest normal form as an automatic goal.
questions.integrity_note: Original MapIT preparation question; not an employer assessment leak.

questions.category: DBA Foundations, Architecture, and Service Management
questions.question: What role do keys and constraints play in database reliability?
questions.preferred_answer: Primary, unique, foreign-key, check, and not-null constraints move critical rules into the database where all clients share them. They improve integrity and optimizer knowledge, but require correct design, deployment sequencing, validation, and monitoring for rejected or orphaned data.
questions.integrity_note: Original MapIT preparation question; not an employer assessment leak.

questions.category: DBA Foundations, Architecture, and Service Management
questions.question: Differentiate DDL, DML, DCL, and transaction-control statements.
questions.preferred_answer: DDL defines structures, DML reads or changes rows, DCL manages privileges, and transaction-control statements define commit, rollback, and savepoint behavior. Product semantics differ, especially whether DDL is transactional, so operational changes must be tested on the target engine.
questions.integrity_note: Original MapIT preparation question; not an employer assessment leak.

questions.category: DBA Foundations, Architecture, and Service Management
questions.question: What is a system catalog or data dictionary?
questions.preferred_answer: It is the database-maintained metadata describing objects, columns, dependencies, privileges, statistics, storage, and operational state. DBAs query it for inventory and diagnosis but should use documented views and interfaces instead of modifying internal catalog tables directly.
questions.integrity_note: Original MapIT preparation question; not an employer assessment leak.

questions.category: DBA Foundations, Architecture, and Service Management
questions.question: What is the difference between a connection and a session?
questions.preferred_answer: A connection is the client-server communication channel; a session is the database context associated with authenticated work, settings, transactions, and temporary state. Some architectures map them one-to-one, while pools and proxies can reuse or multiplex connections, affecting troubleshooting and resource limits.
questions.integrity_note: Original MapIT preparation question; not an employer assessment leak.

questions.category: DBA Foundations, Architecture, and Service Management
questions.question: Why do connection pools matter to a DBA?
questions.preferred_answer: Pools reduce connection setup cost and limit concurrency, but bad sizing can overload the database, hide leaked sessions, retain stale state, and create retry storms. DBAs coordinate limits, timeouts, health checks, transaction cleanup, and observability with application teams.
questions.integrity_note: Original MapIT preparation question; not an employer assessment leak.

questions.category: DBA Foundations, Architecture, and Service Management
questions.question: How does the shared-responsibility model change DBA work in a managed service?
questions.preferred_answer: The provider usually handles selected infrastructure, patching, backups, or failover mechanics, while the customer still owns data design, access, query behavior, configuration choices, retention, validation, monitoring response, and business recovery objectives. The exact boundary must be read for each service and engine.
questions.integrity_note: Original MapIT preparation question; not an employer assessment leak.

questions.category: DBA Foundations, Architecture, and Service Management
questions.question: Define recovery point objective and recovery time objective.
questions.preferred_answer: RPO is the maximum acceptable data loss measured in time; RTO is the maximum acceptable time to restore service. They must be agreed with business owners and then translated into backup frequency, replication mode, automation, staffing, dependency recovery, and tested procedures.
questions.source_title: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 - Contingency Planning Guide
questions.integrity_note: Original MapIT preparation question; not an employer assessment leak.

questions.category: DBA Foundations, Architecture, and Service Management
questions.question: How is an SLA different from an SLO for a database service?
questions.preferred_answer: An SLO is an internal reliability target such as availability or latency; an SLA is a formal commitment that may include remedies. DBAs use measurable indicators and error budgets to manage risk, but must also document exclusions, maintenance, dependencies, and the difference between database uptime and application usability.
questions.integrity_note: Original MapIT preparation question; not an employer assessment leak.

questions.category: DBA Foundations, Architecture, and Service Management
questions.question: What should a database change-management process include?
questions.preferred_answer: It should include purpose, owner, affected systems, prerequisites, risk and blast radius, tested commands, backup or recovery point, maintenance impact, approvals, observability, rollback conditions, validation, communication, and an audit trail. Emergency changes need an accelerated but still documented path.
questions.integrity_note: Original MapIT preparation question; not an employer assessment leak.

questions.category: DBA Foundations, Architecture, and Service Management
questions.question: What makes a DBA runbook useful during an incident?
questions.preferred_answer: A useful runbook states triggers, symptoms, safe diagnostic steps, permissions, decision points, commands with expected output, stop conditions, escalation contacts, communication templates, rollback or recovery paths, and post-action validation. It must be rehearsed and updated after changes and incidents.
questions.source_title: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 - Contingency Planning Guide

questions.category: Data Modeling, Constraints, and Schema Administration
questions.question: Differentiate conceptual, logical, and physical data models.
questions.preferred_answer: A conceptual model captures business entities and relationships, a logical model adds attributes, keys, and normalized structures independent of a product, and a physical model maps the design to engine-specific tables, indexes, partitions, files, and data types. DBAs review the physical model for operability and recovery.
questions.integrity_note: Original MapIT preparation question; not an employer assessment leak.

questions.category: Data Modeling, Constraints, and Schema Administration
questions.question: What problems do the first three normal forms address?
questions.preferred_answer: First normal form removes repeating groups, second normal form removes partial dependency on a composite key, and third normal form removes transitive dependency on non-key attributes. The purpose is to reduce anomalies, not to maximize table count.
questions.integrity_note: Original MapIT preparation question; not an employer assessment leak.

questions.category: Data Modeling, Constraints, and Schema Administration
questions.question: When can denormalization be justified?
questions.preferred_answer: Denormalization can be justified when measured workload evidence shows unacceptable join or aggregation cost and the team can control duplication, refresh, consistency, and recovery. The preferred answer includes ownership, validation, and monitoring rather than using denormalization as the first tuning step.
questions.source_title: Microsoft Learn - Index Architecture and Design Guide
questions.integrity_note: Original MapIT preparation question; not an employer assessment leak.

questions.category: Data Modeling, Constraints, and Schema Administration
questions.question: Compare natural and surrogate primary keys.
questions.preferred_answer: Natural keys carry business meaning but can be wide, mutable, or sensitive. Surrogate keys are compact and stable but require separate uniqueness rules for business identity. The choice should consider change, distribution, integration, indexing, privacy, and operational troubleshooting.
questions.integrity_note: Original MapIT preparation question; not an employer assessment leak.

questions.category: Data Modeling, Constraints, and Schema Administration
questions.question: How is a primary key different from a unique constraint?
questions.preferred_answer: Both enforce uniqueness, but a table has one primary key used as its principal row identity, while it can have multiple unique constraints. Null handling and physical implementation vary by engine. A DBA should preserve semantic intent rather than treating both only as index-creation shortcuts.
questions.integrity_note: Original MapIT preparation question; not an employer assessment leak.

questions.category: Data Modeling, Constraints, and Schema Administration
questions.question: What should be considered before adding a foreign key to a large production table?
questions.preferred_answer: Assess existing orphaned data, lock duration, validation cost, supporting indexes, write overhead, deployment order, cascade behavior, replication, and rollback. Prefer staged validation or online capabilities where supported and monitor blocking and resource usage during the change.
questions.integrity_note: Original MapIT preparation question; not an employer assessment leak.

questions.category: Data Modeling, Constraints, and Schema Administration
questions.question: Why use check constraints instead of only application validation?
questions.preferred_answer: Check constraints protect data regardless of which application, script, import, or administrator writes it. They provide a central rule and may aid optimization. Application validation still improves user experience, but it should not be the only protection for critical invariants.
questions.integrity_note: Original MapIT preparation question; not an employer assessment leak.

questions.category: Data Modeling, Constraints, and Schema Administration
questions.question: Why does NULL require special care in SQL?
questions.preferred_answer: NULL represents unknown or missing information and participates in three-valued logic, so comparisons and aggregates may behave differently from ordinary values. DBAs review nullability, defaults, uniqueness semantics, indexing, and migration logic to prevent silent data-quality errors.
questions.integrity_note: Original MapIT preparation question; not an employer assessment leak.

questions.category: Data Modeling, Constraints, and Schema Administration
questions.question: How do you choose an appropriate data type?
questions.preferred_answer: Choose the type that accurately represents the domain with adequate range and precision while minimizing ambiguity and storage. Consider collation, time zones, decimal versus floating point, length limits, indexing, driver compatibility, migration, and future growth.
questions.integrity_note: Original MapIT preparation question; not an employer assessment leak.

questions.category: Data Modeling, Constraints, and Schema Administration
questions.question: What is the operational impact of character sets and collations?
questions.preferred_answer: Character sets define encoding, while collations define comparison and sort behavior. Changes can affect storage, index size, uniqueness, query results, application compatibility, and migration duration. They must be selected deliberately and tested with multilingual and edge-case data.
questions.integrity_note: Original MapIT preparation question; not an employer assessment leak.

questions.category: Data Modeling, Constraints, and Schema Administration
questions.question: When is table partitioning useful?
questions.preferred_answer: Partitioning is useful when it improves manageability, pruning, retention, loading, or maintenance for large tables. It is not a universal speed feature: poor partition keys, excessive partitions, cross-partition operations, skew, and missing indexes can make performance and operations worse.
questions.integrity_note: Original MapIT preparation question; not an employer assessment leak.

questions.category: Data Modeling, Constraints, and Schema Administration
questions.question: Differentiate a view and a materialized view.
questions.preferred_answer: A view stores a query definition and reads current base data when executed. A materialized view stores results and requires refresh. Materialization can accelerate expensive reads but introduces freshness, storage, refresh locking, dependency, and recovery considerations.
questions.integrity_note: Original MapIT preparation question; not an employer assessment leak.

questions.category: Data Modeling, Constraints, and Schema Administration
questions.question: What are sequences and identity columns used for?
questions.preferred_answer: They generate surrogate values without requiring a client to find the current maximum. They improve concurrency but can produce gaps after rollback, caching, crash, or failover. Applications should not assume gapless business numbering unless a separate controlled process provides it.
questions.integrity_note: Original MapIT preparation question; not an employer assessment leak.

questions.category: Data Modeling, Constraints, and Schema Administration
questions.question: How would you make a backward-compatible schema change?
questions.preferred_answer: Use expand-and-contract: add compatible structures first, deploy code that can handle old and new forms, backfill in controlled batches, verify, switch reads and writes, and remove obsolete structures later. Avoid combining irreversible schema and application changes in one step.
questions.integrity_note: Original MapIT preparation question; not an employer assessment leak.

questions.category: Data Modeling, Constraints, and Schema Administration
questions.question: What does online DDL mean, and why must the term be qualified?
questions.preferred_answer: Online DDL reduces or avoids blocking, but it may still take metadata locks, consume CPU, I/O, log space, temporary space, or briefly block at start or finish. The exact algorithm and limitations vary by engine, object, edition, and version, so test the real operation.
questions.integrity_note: Original MapIT preparation question; not an employer assessment leak.

questions.category: Data Modeling, Constraints, and Schema Administration
questions.question: How do you assess object dependencies before changing or dropping a database object?
questions.preferred_answer: Inspect documented dependency catalogs, application references, stored code, jobs, reports, replication, permissions, synonyms, and external consumers. Capture a baseline, test in a representative environment, communicate deprecation, and preserve a rollback or restore path.
questions.integrity_note: Original MapIT preparation question; not an employer assessment leak.

questions.category: Transactions, Isolation, Locking, and Concurrency
questions.question: What is a database transaction?
questions.preferred_answer: A transaction is a logical unit of work whose changes are committed together or rolled back. It defines a consistency boundary and interacts with isolation, locks or versions, logging, error handling, retries, and application side effects.
questions.integrity_note: Original MapIT preparation question; not an employer assessment leak.

questions.category: Transactions, Isolation, Locking, and Concurrency
questions.question: What do transaction isolation levels control?
questions.preferred_answer: Isolation levels control which concurrent changes a transaction can observe and which anomalies are prevented. Stronger isolation can improve correctness but increase blocking, aborts, or version retention. The correct level depends on the business invariant and engine behavior, not only the level name.
questions.integrity_note: Original MapIT preparation question; not an employer assessment leak.

questions.category: Transactions, Isolation, Locking, and Concurrency
questions.question: Differentiate dirty reads, nonrepeatable reads, and phantom reads.
questions.preferred_answer: A dirty read observes uncommitted data, a nonrepeatable read sees a previously read row change, and a phantom occurs when a repeated predicate returns a different set of rows. Engines may prevent or implement these anomalies differently through locks or MVCC.
questions.integrity_note: Original MapIT preparation question; not an employer assessment leak.

questions.category: Transactions, Isolation, Locking, and Concurrency
questions.question: What is multi-version concurrency control?
questions.preferred_answer: MVCC keeps multiple row versions so readers can use a consistent snapshot without blocking many writers. It improves concurrency but requires cleanup and can retain old versions when transactions or snapshots remain open too long.
questions.integrity_note: Original MapIT preparation question; not an employer assessment leak.

questions.category: Transactions, Isolation, Locking, and Concurrency
questions.question: Compare pessimistic and optimistic concurrency control.
questions.preferred_answer: Pessimistic control locks resources before conflicting work proceeds. Optimistic control allows work and detects conflicts at validation or commit, often using versions. The choice depends on contention, conflict cost, latency, retry safety, and the business rule being protected.
questions.integrity_note: Original MapIT preparation question; not an employer assessment leak.

questions.category: Transactions, Isolation, Locking, and Concurrency
questions.question: How does lock granularity affect concurrency?
questions.preferred_answer: Fine-grained locks allow more concurrency but create more lock-management overhead; coarse locks reduce overhead but block more work. Some engines escalate locks. DBAs examine access patterns, transaction size, indexes, and memory before attempting configuration changes.
questions.source_title: Microsoft Learn - Performance Monitoring and Tuning Tools
questions.integrity_note: Original MapIT preparation question; not an employer assessment leak.

questions.category: Transactions, Isolation, Locking, and Concurrency
questions.question: What is the difference between blocking and a deadlock?
questions.preferred_answer: Blocking is waiting for a resource held by another session and can be normal. A deadlock is a cycle of dependencies in which no participant can progress, so the engine chooses a victim. Diagnosis requires the blocking graph, statements, transactions, and object access order.
questions.integrity_note: Original MapIT preparation question; not an employer assessment leak.

questions.category: Transactions, Isolation, Locking, and Concurrency
questions.question: How should an application handle a deadlock victim?
questions.preferred_answer: Roll back the failed transaction, log enough context, apply bounded retry with jitter only when the operation is safe, and correct the root cause through consistent access order, shorter transactions, better indexes, or reduced scope. Unlimited immediate retries can amplify the incident.
questions.source_title: Microsoft Learn - Performance Monitoring and Tuning Tools
questions.integrity_note: Original MapIT preparation question; not an employer assessment leak.

questions.category: Transactions, Isolation, Locking, and Concurrency
questions.question: Why are long-running transactions operationally risky?
questions.preferred_answer: They retain locks or row versions, delay cleanup, increase log retention, enlarge rollback work, block DDL, and can increase replication or recovery lag. DBAs identify the owner and purpose before terminating them because rollback can itself be expensive.
questions.integrity_note: Original MapIT preparation question; not an employer assessment leak.

questions.category: Transactions, Isolation, Locking, and Concurrency
questions.question: What is autocommit, and when can it cause surprises?
questions.preferred_answer: Autocommit commits each statement unless an explicit transaction is opened. It can prevent grouping related changes or unexpectedly keep transactions open when drivers change behavior. DBAs and developers must understand driver defaults and always close or roll back failed work.
questions.integrity_note: Original MapIT preparation question; not an employer assessment leak.

questions.category: Transactions, Isolation, Locking, and Concurrency
questions.question: What is a savepoint?
questions.preferred_answer: A savepoint marks a point inside a transaction to which part of the work can be rolled back without ending the whole transaction. It helps complex workflows but does not replace clear error handling and can extend transaction duration and resource retention.
questions.integrity_note: Original MapIT preparation question; not an employer assessment leak.

questions.category: Transactions, Isolation, Locking, and Concurrency
questions.question: What is two-phase commit, and what operational risk does it introduce?
questions.preferred_answer: Two-phase commit prepares participating transactions before a final commit decision, supporting atomic work across resources. If the coordinator or communication fails, prepared transactions can remain in doubt and hold resources, requiring durable coordination records and recovery procedures.
questions.integrity_note: Original MapIT preparation question; not an employer assessment leak.

questions.category: Transactions, Isolation, Locking, and Concurrency
questions.question: Why is idempotency important when retrying database work?
questions.preferred_answer: An idempotent operation can be repeated without creating unintended additional effects. Retries after timeouts may occur even when the original commit succeeded, so use stable request identifiers, uniqueness constraints, conditional updates, or transactional outbox patterns.
questions.integrity_note: Original MapIT preparation question; not an employer assessment leak.

questions.category: Transactions, Isolation, Locking, and Concurrency
questions.question: What is write skew under snapshot isolation?
questions.preferred_answer: Write skew occurs when concurrent transactions read a consistent snapshot, update different rows, and together violate a cross-row invariant. Prevent it with serializable isolation, explicit locking, materialized constraints, or redesign that makes the conflict visible to the database.
questions.integrity_note: Original MapIT preparation question; not an employer assessment leak.

questions.category: Transactions, Isolation, Locking, and Concurrency
questions.question: What is the transaction log used for?
questions.preferred_answer: The log records changes in an order that supports durability, crash recovery, rollback, replication, and point-in-time recovery. It must be protected, sized, backed up or archived as required, and monitored because a full or unavailable log can stop writes.
questions.integrity_note: Original MapIT preparation question; not an employer assessment leak.

questions.category: Transactions, Isolation, Locking, and Concurrency
questions.question: How would you diagnose a blocking incident safely?
questions.preferred_answer: Capture the head blocker, waiting chain, statements, transaction age, lock types, application identity, and resource pressure before acting. Contact the owner where possible, avoid killing arbitrary sessions, estimate rollback, preserve evidence, and verify recovery after any intervention.
questions.integrity_note: Original MapIT preparation question; not an employer assessment leak.

questions.category: Physical Storage, Memory, Logging, and I/O
questions.question: What are database pages or blocks?
questions.preferred_answer: Pages or blocks are fixed-size units in which the engine reads, writes, caches, and manages table or index data. Their structure is engine-specific, but understanding them helps explain I/O, fragmentation, row size, checksums, and corruption messages.
questions.source_title: Microsoft Learn - Pages and Extents Architecture Guide
questions.integrity_note: Original MapIT preparation question; not an employer assessment leak.

questions.category: Physical Storage, Memory, Logging, and I/O
questions.question: What are tablespaces, filegroups, and datafiles?
questions.preferred_answer: They are physical or logical storage containers used to place database objects across files and storage. Names and capabilities differ by engine. DBAs use them for capacity, backup, recovery, I/O placement, lifecycle, and administrative boundaries, not as substitutes for proper workload design.
questions.integrity_note: Original MapIT preparation question; not an employer assessment leak.

questions.category: Physical Storage, Memory, Logging, and I/O
questions.question: Compare a heap and a clustered storage structure.
questions.preferred_answer: A heap stores rows without ordering by a clustered key, while a clustered structure organizes data rows by an index key or equivalent. Heaps can suit staging or append patterns, but forwarded rows, scans, and lookup behavior must be measured on the target engine.
questions.source_title: Microsoft Learn - Index Architecture and Design Guide
questions.integrity_note: Original MapIT preparation question; not an employer assessment leak.

questions.category: Physical Storage, Memory, Logging, and I/O
questions.question: How do row-oriented and column-oriented storage differ?
questions.preferred_answer: Row storage keeps values from one row together and suits selective transactional access. Column storage keeps values by column and improves compression and analytical scans. Hybrid systems require DBAs to match storage format, indexing, load pattern, memory, and maintenance to the workload.
questions.source_title: Microsoft Learn - Index Architecture and Design Guide
questions.integrity_note: Original MapIT preparation question; not an employer assessment leak.

questions.category: Physical Storage, Memory, Logging, and I/O
questions.question: Differentiate redo, undo, and write-ahead logging.
questions.preferred_answer: Redo records changes needed to reapply committed work during recovery. Undo supports rollback or older versions. Write-ahead logging requires the relevant log record to be durable before the changed data page. Product terminology differs, but the durability principle is consistent.
questions.integrity_note: Original MapIT preparation question; not an employer assessment leak.

questions.category: Physical Storage, Memory, Logging, and I/O
questions.question: What is a checkpoint?
questions.preferred_answer: A checkpoint coordinates flushing or recording dirty-state progress so crash recovery has a bounded starting point. Frequent checkpoints can increase write pressure; infrequent checkpoints can increase recovery work and log retention. Tuning must consider workload and durability.
questions.integrity_note: Original MapIT preparation question; not an employer assessment leak.

questions.category: Physical Storage, Memory, Logging, and I/O
questions.question: What is the database buffer cache?
questions.preferred_answer: It is memory used to cache database pages and reduce physical I/O. A high hit ratio alone does not prove health; DBAs also examine working-set fit, read latency, write pressure, scan patterns, OS caching, and whether memory is being stolen by other components.
questions.integrity_note: Original MapIT preparation question; not an employer assessment leak.

questions.category: Physical Storage, Memory, Logging, and I/O
questions.question: What is temporary database space used for?
questions.preferred_answer: Temporary space supports sorts, hashes, intermediate results, version stores, temporary tables, and maintenance. Unexpected growth can indicate spills, poor plans, long transactions, or large operations. It needs capacity, monitoring, and workload-specific controls.
questions.source_title: Microsoft Learn - SQL Server Database Engine
questions.integrity_note: Original MapIT preparation question; not an employer assessment leak.

questions.category: Physical Storage, Memory, Logging, and I/O
questions.question: Why can transaction-log growth become an outage?
questions.preferred_answer: The log may grow when backups, archiving, replication, long transactions, or checkpoints cannot advance reuse. Unlimited growth can fill storage; too-small growth increments can create repeated stalls. DBAs diagnose the reuse blocker before shrinking or deleting anything.
questions.source_title: Microsoft Learn - Back up and Restore SQL Server Databases
questions.integrity_note: Original MapIT preparation question; not an employer assessment leak.

questions.category: Physical Storage, Memory, Logging, and I/O
questions.question: How should database file autogrowth be configured?
questions.preferred_answer: Use deliberate fixed increments or suitable policies, sufficient preallocation, monitored free space, and storage with predictable latency. Very small increments cause frequent pauses and fragmentation; unlimited growth without alerts can exhaust the volume.
questions.source_title: Microsoft Learn - Pages and Extents Architecture Guide
questions.integrity_note: Original MapIT preparation question; not an employer assessment leak.

questions.category: Physical Storage, Memory, Logging, and I/O
questions.question: Differentiate index fragmentation and table bloat.
questions.preferred_answer: Fragmentation describes inefficient physical page organization or free space; bloat often describes retained or unused space from versioned updates and deletes. The terms and remedies differ by engine. Measure impact before rebuilding, reorganizing, vacuuming, or rewriting.
questions.integrity_note: Original MapIT preparation question; not an employer assessment leak.

questions.category: Physical Storage, Memory, Logging, and I/O
questions.question: What are the trade-offs of database compression?
questions.preferred_answer: Compression reduces storage and I/O but consumes CPU and can change maintenance, backup, and licensing requirements. Evaluate row shape, workload, cache benefit, write amplification, recovery speed, and platform support using representative tests.
questions.source_title: Microsoft Learn - Index Architecture and Design Guide
questions.integrity_note: Original MapIT preparation question; not an employer assessment leak.

questions.category: Physical Storage, Memory, Logging, and I/O
questions.question: How should large objects be handled?
questions.preferred_answer: Choose in-row, out-of-row, or external object storage based on size, transactionality, access pattern, backup, replication, security, and retention. Avoid placing large objects in the database by habit or excluding them by habit; test the complete operational lifecycle.
questions.integrity_note: Original MapIT preparation question; not an employer assessment leak.

questions.category: Physical Storage, Memory, Logging, and I/O
questions.question: Differentiate IOPS, throughput, and latency.
questions.preferred_answer: IOPS is operations per second, throughput is data transferred per second, and latency is time per operation. Database workloads can be limited by any combination, and averages can hide queueing or tail latency. Match metrics to read/write size and concurrency.

questions.category: Physical Storage, Memory, Logging, and I/O
questions.question: How much free storage headroom should a database have?
questions.preferred_answer: There is no universal percentage. Headroom must cover normal growth, temporary operations, log expansion, maintenance, failover, restores, and alert-response time. Use growth trends, peak events, storage limits, and business lead time to set warning and critical thresholds.

questions.category: Physical Storage, Memory, Logging, and I/O
questions.question: Differentiate physical corruption from logical inconsistency.
questions.preferred_answer: Physical corruption means pages, blocks, checksums, or files cannot be trusted. Logical inconsistency means validly stored data violates intended relationships or business rules. Response differs: preserve evidence, stop harmful writes, assess scope, use integrity tools, restore or repair carefully, and validate at the application level.

questions.question: What problem does an index solve?

questions.question: How does a B-tree index work conceptually?

questions.question: What are cardinality and selectivity?

questions.question: What is a covering index or index-only scan?

practical_scenarios.title: Production volume is 98% full
practical_scenarios.situation: The primary database volume is growing rapidly. The transaction log and temporary space share the same storage, and writes may stop within an hour.
practical_scenarios.candidate_task: Describe immediate containment, diagnosis, communication, and durable remediation without deleting unknown files.
practical_scenarios.preferred_response: Confirm the growth source and exact free space, protect the log chain, pause nonessential bulk work, extend or add approved storage, and identify log reuse, temp, or object growth. Do not shrink or delete database files blindly. Set explicit thresholds, forecast, and verify backups, replication, and application writes after stabilization.
practical_scenarios.escalation_communication: State affected services, estimated time to exhaustion, current containment, data-risk level, required infrastructure decision, next update time, and long-term owner.
practical_scenarios.source_title: Microsoft Learn - Pages and Extents Architecture Guide
practical_scenarios.integrity_note: Original MapIT scenario; not a leaked employer case.

practical_scenarios.title: CPU saturation after a release
practical_scenarios.situation: Database CPU rose from 35% to 95% immediately after an application release while I/O latency remains normal.
practical_scenarios.candidate_task: Explain how you would isolate whether the cause is query volume, plan regression, compilation, or application behavior.
practical_scenarios.preferred_response: Correlate release time, throughput, top statements, plans, parameters, compile rate, waits, connection behavior, and errors. Compare the prior baseline, mitigate with rollback or targeted plan/query action, and avoid killing random sessions. Validate user transactions and continue observation.
practical_scenarios.escalation_communication: Communicate confirmed correlation, impact, mitigation choice, rollback decision owner, data-safety status, and next update.
practical_scenarios.source_title: Microsoft Learn - Tune Performance with Query Store
practical_scenarios.integrity_note: Original MapIT scenario; not a leaked employer case.

practical_scenarios.title: One session blocks hundreds of requests
practical_scenarios.situation: A long transaction from a batch job is the head blocker for an online order system.
practical_scenarios.candidate_task: Decide whether to wait, cancel, or terminate it and how to reduce risk.
practical_scenarios.preferred_response: Capture the blocking chain, transaction age, SQL, owner, completed work, rollback estimate, log and replica impact, and business criticality. Stop new batch work, contact the owner, choose the least harmful action, monitor rollback, and correct transaction scope, indexing, or schedule.
practical_scenarios.escalation_communication: Report head blocker, affected workload, chosen action and risk, expected rollback or recovery time, and prevention owner.
practical_scenarios.integrity_note: Original MapIT scenario; not a leaked employer case.

practical_scenarios.title: Deadlocks spike during peak traffic
practical_scenarios.situation: The application retries deadlock victims immediately and error volume is increasing.
practical_scenarios.candidate_task: Provide a technical and operational response.
practical_scenarios.preferred_response: Capture deadlock graphs and identify the repeated access cycle, tables, indexes, and transaction order. Apply bounded retries with jitter, reduce transaction scope, use consistent object order, and fix missing access paths. Rate-limit retry storms and verify business idempotency.
practical_scenarios.escalation_communication: Explain that the database remains consistent, quantify failed or retried transactions, state mitigation, and identify any user actions requiring reconciliation.
practical_scenarios.source_title: Microsoft Learn - Performance Monitoring and Tuning Tools
practical_scenarios.integrity_note: Original MapIT scenario; not a leaked employer case.

practical_scenarios.title: Backups have silently failed for three days
practical_scenarios.situation: Monitoring shows success, but the backup destination has rejected writes and no valid recent backup exists.
practical_scenarios.candidate_task: Describe the first hour and the recovery-risk decision.
practical_scenarios.preferred_response: Confirm the latest restorable chain and log retention, preserve existing copies, fix destination or create an alternate approved backup immediately, test or verify it, assess RPO exposure, and review why monitoring missed the failure. Do not claim safety until a restore path is proven.
practical_scenarios.escalation_communication: Escalate the recovery-point breach, affected databases, latest valid point, current corrective backup, business acceptance of risk, and next restore-test milestone.
practical_scenarios.source_title: AWS - Backing up and Restoring Amazon RDS
practical_scenarios.integrity_note: Original MapIT scenario; not a leaked employer case.

practical_scenarios.title: A user deleted critical rows
practical_scenarios.situation: A valid administrative command deleted data from one business table 20 minutes ago, and replication has already applied it.
practical_scenarios.candidate_task: Choose among rollback, flashback, PITR, logical recovery, and application reconstruction.
practical_scenarios.preferred_response: Stop further harmful writes if necessary, identify the exact transaction and dependent changes, preserve logs and backups, and restore or flash back in an isolated environment to extract the minimum correct data. Reconcile keys and downstream effects before controlled reintroduction.
practical_scenarios.escalation_communication: Communicate the affected period and data set, containment, expected recovery path, uncertainty, and validation owner without blaming the operator.

practical_scenarios.title: Replica lag threatens RPO
practical_scenarios.situation: A disaster-recovery replica is 45 minutes behind and lag continues to grow during a data load.
practical_scenarios.candidate_task: Diagnose and decide whether to pause the load, scale, or accept temporary risk.
practical_scenarios.preferred_response: Separate send, receive, and apply lag; inspect transaction size, locks, indexes, I/O, CPU, network, and replay errors. Compare lag with the agreed RPO, pause or throttle nonessential load, protect log retention, and restore healthy apply before making architectural changes.
practical_scenarios.escalation_communication: Report current lag, RPO breach or risk, source workload, containment, estimated catch-up, and business decision required.

practical_scenarios.preferred_response: Confirm the new primary and fencing, validate listener or DNS and network rules, expire or recycle stale pools safely, test credentials and a business transaction, and monitor retries. Preserve evidence of whether any writes reached the old primary.
practical_scenarios.escalation_communication: Distinguish database role health from application availability, state the routing issue, data-safety status, recovery steps, and next validation.

practical_scenarios.title: Integrity check reports page corruption

practical_scenarios.candidate_task: Describe evidence preservation, containment, and recovery choices.
practical_scenarios.preferred_response: Preserve full error output and logs, identify affected objects and storage signals, stop risky maintenance, assess readable data and replica copies, take a tail or protective backup if appropriate, and prioritize restore from a known clean backup over repair with data loss. Validate at database and application levels.
practical_scenarios.escalation_communication: Escalate as a data-integrity incident, state known scope and uncertainty, protective actions, recovery options, and decision owner.

practical_scenarios.title: An index deployment caused a workload regression

practical_scenarios.candidate_task: Decide whether to retain, modify, or roll back the index.
practical_scenarios.preferred_response: Compare full workload reads, CPU, DML cost, storage, log generation, lag, and plan changes. If user impact is severe, remove or disable through the approved rollback. Consider a narrower composite, filtered, covering, or reporting-specific alternative and retest.
practical_scenarios.escalation_communication: Explain the trade-off, affected workloads, rollback status, report mitigation, and follow-up design owner.

practical_scenarios.title: A database credential appears in a public repository
practical_scenarios.situation: A production service-account password with write access was committed to a public code repository.
practical_scenarios.preferred_response: Revoke or rotate the credential immediately using a coordinated rollout, inspect audit and connection logs for misuse, restrict network paths, preserve repository and database evidence, review privilege scope, rotate related secrets if needed, and migrate to managed secret handling.
practical_scenarios.escalation_communication: Treat it as a security incident, state exposure window, privileges, evidence status, containment, affected owners, and next investigation update.

practical_scenarios.title: A privileged role was granted without approval
practical_scenarios.situation: An application login was added to a database-owner or superuser-equivalent role during troubleshooting and never removed.

practical_scenarios.preferred_response: Capture current grants, grantor, timing, sessions, and activity; determine required permissions; replace broad access with a narrow role; revoke elevated membership; validate application function; and review similar accounts and the approval process.
practical_scenarios.escalation_communication: Report the unauthorized privilege, exposure period, observed usage, remediation, validation, and governance corrective action.

practical_scenarios.title: Migration cutover is missing its window
practical_scenarios.situation: Initial data is loaded, but change-capture lag is 40 minutes and the business-approved outage has 20 minutes remaining.
practical_scenarios.candidate_task: Make a go, delay, or abort recommendation.
practical_scenarios.preferred_response: Compare lag and catch-up rate with the cutover and rollback deadlines, validate source stability, identify bottlenecks, and avoid forcing cutover with unknown divergence. Recommend delay or abort unless the remaining plan can meet integrity and validation criteria. Preserve the source as authoritative.
practical_scenarios.escalation_communication: State the objective evidence, remaining time, data-consistency risk, recommendation, business decision owner, and revised plan.

practical_scenarios.title: Managed database cost doubles unexpectedly

practical_scenarios.candidate_task: Reduce cost without creating recovery or availability gaps.
practical_scenarios.preferred_response: Break down compute, storage, I/O, backup, transfer, and licensing; identify unused resources and retention beyond policy; verify replica purposes; right-size using workload evidence; and protect RPO, RTO, and peak capacity. practical_scenarios.escalation_communication: Provide immediate savings, reliability trade-offs, approvals, and a monitoring plan that detects recurrence.

practical_scenarios.candidate_task: Break the queue safely and prevent recurrence.
practical_scenarios.preferred_response: Identify the old transaction, queued DDL, affected sessions, rollback cost, and deployment timeout. Cancel the DDL or terminate the blocker according to the lower-risk path, stop new deployment attempts, and redesign with preflight checks, lock timeouts, smaller changes, and transaction hygiene.

practical_scenarios.escalation_communication: Report that database media recovery succeeded but service recovery is incomplete, list missing dependencies, owners, expected completion, and residual risks.
